headline: Ancient Fire Practice Revives 140 Million Hectares Across Australia
meta_description: The Indigenous Desert Alliance uses ancestral cultural burning practices to restore biodiversity across one-third of Australia, protecting wildlife and prevent…
summary_short: Aboriginal rangers across Australia's desert are reviving thousands-year-old fire management techniques, restoring vast ecosystems while preventing destructive wildfires.
body:
Across one-third of Australia, 885 Indigenous rangers are bringing ancestral knowledge back to the land through a practice older than written history. The Indigenous Desert Alliance—a network of 70 ranger teams spanning 270 million hectares of desert, an area almost as large as Argentina—has restored biodiversity to 140 million hectares over the past four years using cultural burning, a management technique passed down through Aboriginal culture for millennia. The work has earned the alliance a nomination for an Earthshot Prize, recognition of what is now the world's largest Indigenous-led conservation corridor.

Cultural burning works through careful, deliberate application of fire guided by Traditional Owners—Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people with ancestral, physical, or spiritual ties to the land. Unlike the chaotic, destructive wildfires of Australia's hot summers, these controlled burns manage fuel loads, allow plants to renew themselves, and protect wildlife habitats. The knowledge flows not through manuals or handbooks, but through oral storytelling and what rangers call "yarns"—collaborative dialogues shared on Country, the Indigenous concept of a living entity encompassing land, waters, skies, and all living things. Ranger Scott West, for example, guides burning exercises from a plane after learning the practice on the ground from elders and uncles who pointed out exactly where and how to burn.

Samantha Murray, CEO of the Indigenous Desert Alliance, emphasizes that this work belongs to all Australians. "We're caring for such a big part of Australia, like a third of Australia," she says, urging people to recognize the "really committed professional people" working on the ground. The rangers are not simply preserving Indigenous land—they are stewarding ecosystems that sustain the nation's wildlife and protect communities from catastrophic fire.
quick_facts: 70 ranger teams manage 270 million hectares—larger than Argentina
885 Indigenous rangers restored 140 million hectares in four years
Cultural burning knowledge passed down through oral storytelling and yarns
Covers approximately one-third of Australia's total land area
Prevents summer wildfires while allowing plant and animal regeneration
